title: Origins & Early Religions
description: From animism to ancient state religions

concepts.title: Prehistoric and Ancient Religions
concepts.contentHtml:
Religion appears archaeologically in burial practices (~100,000 years ago) and cave art (~40,000 years ago). Early religions were likely animistic — spirits in nature, ancestral spirits, ritual practitioners (shamans).

With agricultural civilizations came organized state religions: Mesopotamian polytheism, Egyptian pharaonic religion with its elaborate afterlife focus, Greek Olympian religion. Religion legitimized rulers, organized agricultural cycles, gave meaning to suffering and death.

concepts.title: The Axial Age
concepts.contentHtml:
Karl Jaspers's 'Axial Age' (~800-200 BCE) saw simultaneous religious and philosophical revolutions across Eurasia: Greek philosophy, Hebrew prophets, Indian sages (Buddha, Mahavira), Confucius and Laozi in China, Zoroaster in Persia.

Common themes: ethical inwardness, transcendent or universal claims, individual salvation/liberation. Earlier ritual-focused religions gave way to ethically focused traditions — though ritual remained.

Whether the simultaneity is real or coincidental is debated. The intellectual and moral foundations of most modern religions and philosophies trace to this period.

concepts.title: Hinduism
concepts.contentHtml:
Hinduism is the world's oldest continuously practiced major religion, with roots ~3000 BCE. Not a single founder or central doctrine — a family of traditions sharing concepts (dharma, karma, samsara, moksha) and texts (Vedas, Upanishads, Bhagavad Gita).

Polytheistic in popular practice (~330 million deities), often understood as manifestations of one ultimate reality (Brahman). Major schools include Vaishnavism (Vishnu-focused), Shaivism (Shiva-focused), Shaktism (Devi-focused).

~1.2 billion adherents, mostly in India and Nepal. Has influenced global culture extensively (yoga, vegetarianism, Hindu-derived language and concepts).

concepts.title: The Buddha and Buddhist Origins
concepts.contentHtml:
Siddhartha Gautama (~563-483 BCE) — born a prince in northern India/Nepal, became the Buddha ('awakened one'). His teachings: the Four Noble Truths (life is suffering; suffering arises from attachment; cessation of attachment ends suffering; the Eightfold Path leads to cessation).

Three Refuges: the Buddha (the teacher), the Dharma (the teaching), the Sangha (the community).

Buddhism rejects the eternal soul, caste-based authority, and Vedic ritualism. It spread through India and across Asia after Emperor Ashoka's patronage (~250 BCE).

concepts.title: Buddhist Schools & Spread
concepts.contentHtml:
Three major Buddhist traditions today:

• Theravada ('Way of the Elders'): emphasizes the Pali canon and individual monastic practice. Dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia.
• Mahayana ('Great Vehicle'): emphasizes bodhisattva ideal, lay practice, broader scriptures. Dominant in China, Japan, Korea, Vietnam.
• Vajrayana ('Diamond Vehicle'): tantric Buddhism with elaborate ritual. Dominant in Tibet, Mongolia, Bhutan.

~500 million Buddhists today. Notably, Buddhism largely declined in its Indian birthplace after the medieval period.

concepts.title: Confucianism and Daoism
concepts.contentHtml:
Confucianism: ethical-political teachings of Confucius (~551-479 BCE) emphasizing virtue, hierarchical relationships, ritual propriety (li), and humanity (ren). Shaped Chinese society for over 2000 years.

Daoism (Taoism): associated with Laozi (~6th century BCE) and the Dao De Jing. Emphasizes harmony with the Dao (way), naturalness, non-action (wu wei). Religious Daoism developed elaborate rituals, immortality practices, deities.

Most East Asians historically practiced a syncretic blend of Confucianism, Daoism, Buddhism, and folk religion. Strict separation is more a Western category than an Asian reality.

concepts.title: Judaism
concepts.contentHtml:
Judaism is the oldest of the Abrahamic religions, traceable to ancient Israel (~13th-12th century BCE). Monotheistic — one God who chose the Israelites for covenant relationship. Sacred texts: Hebrew Bible (Tanakh), Talmud, rabbinic literature.

The destruction of the Second Temple (70 CE) ended sacrificial Judaism; rabbinic Judaism emerged with synagogues, Torah study, halakha (Jewish law) as organizing principles.

Modern Judaism: ~15 million adherents, branches include Orthodox, Conservative, Reform, Reconstructionist. Holocaust (1933-45) killed ~6 million Jews; Israel founded 1948.

concepts.title: Christianity
concepts.contentHtml:
Christianity began as a Jewish sect following Jesus of Nazareth (~4 BCE-30 CE), who was crucified by Roman authorities. Followers held him to be the Messiah (Christ) and the Son of God; his resurrection central to their faith.

Paul's missionary work spread the religion across the Roman Empire. Christianity was legalized by Constantine (313 CE) and became the state religion under Theodosius (380 CE).

Major splits: Great Schism (1054) between Catholic and Eastern Orthodox; Reformation (1517+) between Catholic and Protestant. ~2.4 billion adherents today — the world's largest religion.

concepts.title: Islam
concepts.contentHtml:
Islam was founded by Muhammad in 7th-century Arabia (covered in detail in the Islamic World History topic). Quran and Hadith are central scriptures.

Common Abrahamic threads: monotheism, prophetic tradition (Abraham, Moses, Jesus all recognized in Islam), eschatology, ethical demands.

The three Abrahamic religions together account for ~55% of humanity. Their relationship — sometimes peaceful coexistence, sometimes violent conflict — has shaped world history for over a millennium.

title: Religion and Power
description: How religions intersected with politics across history

concepts.title: State Religions
concepts.contentHtml:
Many states established official religions: Roman imperial religion, Christianity in Byzantium and most of Europe post-Constantine, Islam in caliphates, Confucianism in imperial China.

State religion provided ideological legitimacy — rulers ruled by divine sanction. It also generated tensions — between religious and secular authority, among different sects, between rulers and theologians.

Modern secular states (US, France post-Revolution, Turkey, India) explicitly separate religion from government — though the practice varies enormously.

concepts.title: Reformation & Wars of Religion
concepts.contentHtml:
Martin Luther's 1517 Ninety-Five Theses challenged Catholic indulgences and launched the Protestant Reformation. Vernacular Bibles, justification by faith alone, priesthood of all believers — the religious landscape of Europe transformed.

The Wars of Religion (1524-1648) ravaged Europe. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) established the principle cuius regio, eius religio — each ruler determines their territory's religion. Modern sovereign-state system traces partly to this peace.

The Reformation spawned numerous Protestant denominations (Lutheran, Calvinist, Anglican, etc.) and indirectly stimulated science, capitalism, and secular thought.

concepts.title: Religion and Colonialism
concepts.contentHtml:
European colonialism was deeply intertwined with Christian missionary activity. Spanish conquistadors brought Catholic missions; Protestant powers brought their own missionaries.

Religious conversion was often coerced or strongly encouraged. Indigenous religions were suppressed. Yet Christianity also took root deeply, becoming the majority religion of Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, and other former colonial regions.

Modern global Christianity is increasingly non-Western. The largest Christian populations are in Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa, not Europe.

concepts.title: Secularization
concepts.contentHtml:
The 'secularization thesis' predicted religion would decline as societies modernized. In Europe and East Asia, this has largely been true — religious affiliation, attendance, and belief have all dropped.

But globally, religion remains strong and growing. The US has remained more religious than most rich countries. Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa are deeply Christian; the Middle East and South Asia deeply Muslim.

Refined view: secularization happens unevenly. Educated urban populations in many societies are increasingly secular; rural populations and the developing world often remain religious.

concepts.title: Fundamentalism
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern fundamentalist movements — Christian, Islamic, Hindu, Jewish — share features: literalism about scripture, opposition to liberal modernity, tight community boundaries, political activism.

Often appears most strongly when traditional religion meets rapid social change. American Protestant fundamentalism (early 20th c.); Saudi Wahhabism; Khomeinist Iran; Hindutva in India; ultra-Orthodox Judaism in Israel.

Fundamentalism is a modern phenomenon, not a return to pre-modernity. Its political and cultural impacts are major in many parts of the world.

concepts.title: New Religious Movements
concepts.contentHtml:
Modern religious creativity is vast. Mormonism (1830s), Bahá'í (1844), Pentecostalism (early 1900s, now ~600 million adherents — a quarter of all Christians), Scientology (1950s), and many others have emerged.

The 'spiritual but not religious' demographic is large in much of the developed world. Yoga, mindfulness meditation, secular Buddhism — Eastern practices repackaged for Western consumers.

Religion's ultimate fate is uncertain. Some scholars see it as a permanent feature of human cognition; others predict continued decline. Either way, religion will continue to shape much of the world for the foreseeable future.
